reference_title: California Trenching and Shoring Manual (Caltrans, June 2011, Revision 2 - July 2025)
chapter_title: Construction Considerations and Final Summary (incl. Ground Anchor Restrained Shoring Systems)

sections.title: Ground Anchor Restrained Shoring Systems (Overview)
sections.summary: Restrained shoring is higher risk: it usually retains greater soil heights, has additional elements that must perform as intended, is sensitive to the installation/removal sequence, and involves drilling/disturbance below or behind the wall (utility damage risk). This section focuses on ground anchors (tiebacks) as the restraining element.
sections.body: Restrained shoring systems are generally considered higher risk due to several factors. First, these systems are often retaining a greater height of soil. Another risk is the additional elements of the system that must perform as intended, and that the sequence of installation and removal affects the loading and performance of the shoring system. There are also risks involved with additional drilling or disturbance below or behind the shoring, such as damaging utilities. This section focuses specifically on ground anchors used as a restraining element.
key_points: Restrained (anchored) shoring is higher risk than unrestrained shoring
Risks: greater retained height, additional elements that must perform, installation/removal sequence sensitivity, drilling disturbance and utility damage
Section 11-3 covers ground anchors (tiebacks) as the restraining element
sections.applicability: Understanding the added risks of ground-anchor (tieback) restrained shoring systems

sections.title: Engineering Analysis and Construction Sequence
sections.summary: The construction sequence of a restrained system (sheet or soldier pile) must be considered in the engineering analysis whether the restraint is a strut, a buried anchor block, or a drilled ground anchor. Different loads act before and after each level of intermediate support is completed, so each installation stage should be analyzed - and each stage of support removal during backfilling may also need analysis.
sections.body: The construction sequence for a restrained shoring system, sheet pile or soldier pile, must be considered when making an engineering analysis. This is true whether the restraint is strutting, a buried anchor block, or a drilled ground anchor. Different loads are imposed on the system before and after the completion of a level of intermediate supports. An analysis for each stage of the system's installation should be performed, and an analysis for each stage of support removal during backfilling operations may also be needed.
key_points: The construction sequence must be part of the engineering analysis (struts, anchor blocks, or drilled anchors)
Loads differ before and after each intermediate support level is completed
Analyze each installation stage; analyze each support-removal stage during backfilling as needed
sections.applicability: Staging the analysis of a restrained shoring system through installation and removal

sections.title: Components of Ground Anchor Systems
sections.summary: Ground anchor components: piling (sheet/soldier piles); walers transferring earth pressure to the anchor (33% overstress allowed during proof testing; anchors often go directly through pile flanges, needing stiffeners/cover plates and a cut-section analysis); the tendon (high-strength bars/strands, centered with centralizers); stress limits (Fpu = 150 ksi bars, 270 ksi strand; Ft <= 0.6 Fpu at design load and <= 0.8 Fpu at proof load, both must be checked; the design load applies a safety factor of 1.3 to the proof load); and grout (neat cement up to 8-in holes, sand-cement >= 8 in, aggregate concrete for very large holes; Type I/II, Type III for high early strength; inject from the bottom).
sections.body: There are many variations of ground anchor systems. The tension element may be prestressing strands or bars, single or multiple elements; ground anchors may be secured against walers or piles. Figure 11-1 illustrates a typical temporary ground anchor (a bar tendon system; strand systems are similar). Common components: PILING - sheet piling and soldier piles (see Chapter 6 for materials and allowable stresses). WALER - transfers the resultant earth pressure from the piling to the ground anchor; an overstress of 33 percent to the allowable design value is permitted for walers when proof testing the anchor. Temporary anchors are often anchored directly against the soldier piling through holes or slots in the flanges, eliminating walers; bearing stiffeners and flange cover plates are generally added to compensate for the loss of section, and a structural analysis of this cut section should always be required. TENDON - generally the same high-strength bars or strands used in prestressing concrete; anchorage consists of bearing plates and anchor nuts (bar tendons) or bearing plates, anchor head, and strand wedges (strand tendons), with shims/wedge plates accommodating the anchor inclination. The tendon should be centered within the drilled hole throughout its length using centralizers (spacers) or a hollow-stem auger. STRESS - allowable tensile stresses are a percentage of the ultimate tensile strength Fpu (bars Fpu = 150 ksi, strand Fpu = 270 ksi; check manufacturer data): at design load Ft <= 0.6 Fpu, at proof load Ft <= 0.8 Fpu (both conditions must be checked). The relationship between proof load and design load can be thought of in this manner: the proof load provides a value that could be considered the maximum value to use for the soil, and the design load applies a safety factor of 1.3 to the proof load (Table 11-1 recommends proof test loads of 1.2 to 1.3 of the design load for normal risk and >= 1.3 for high risk). GROUT - a flowable Portland cement grout or concrete encapsulates the tendon and fills the hole within the bonded length; neat cement grout for holes up to 8 in diameter, sand-cement for >= 8 in, aggregate concrete for very large holes; Type I or II cement (Type III for high early strength). Grout should, with few exceptions, always be injected at the bottom of the hole to ensure complete grouting and displace accumulated water.
key_points: Components: piling, waler, tendon (bar or strand), grout
Waler transfers earth pressure to the anchor; 33% overstress allowed during proof testing
Anchors often go directly through pile flanges (add stiffeners/cover plates; analyze the cut section)
Stress limits: Fpu = 150 ksi (bars), 270 ksi (strand); Ft <= 0.6 Fpu at design load, <= 0.8 Fpu at proof load (both checked)
The design load applies a safety factor of 1.3 to the proof load (p. 11-8); Table 11-1 proof loads: 1.2-1.3 (normal risk), >= 1.3 (high risk) x design
Center the tendon with centralizers/spacers; grout from the bottom of the hole
Grout: neat cement to 8-in holes, sand-cement >= 8 in, aggregate concrete for very large holes; Type I/II (III for high early strength)

equations.description: Allowable tendon tensile stress at design load Ft <= 0.6 Fpu (Fpu = 150 ksi bars, 270 ksi strand).
Allowable tendon tensile stress at proof load Ft <= 0.8 Fpu (both the design-load and proof-load conditions must be checked).

sections.title: Ground Anchor (Capacity, Bond, Unbonded Length)
sections.summary: Anchor capacity depends on many interrelated factors and is confirmed by proof/performance tests. Most temporary anchors are straight-shafted with low-pressure (tremie) grout. Bond (pull-out) capacity develops along the bonded length. Ultimate capacity Pult = pi*d*Lb*Sb (hole diameter d, bonded length Lb, bond strength Sb). The Engineer checks the unbonded length: the front of the bonded zone must be >= H/5 (and >= 5 ft) beyond the active failure surface, and Lu >= 15 ft. Bond strength depends on overburden, drilling method/hole shape, soil, grouting method/pressure, and tendon. Post-grouting (>= 150 psi) increases capacity; under-reamed (belled) holes need cohesive soil.
sections.body: There are several types of ground anchors; capacity depends on a number of interrelated factors. Alternative products (e.g., CHANCE Helical screw anchors, Manta Ray deadman-style earth anchors) follow the manufacturer's published data. The most typical drilled hole is a straight-shafted hole; occasionally a hole is mechanically enlarged (under-reamed/belled) to add bearing, which requires soils with sufficient cohesion to prevent collapse (Figure 11-2). Water (drilling-introduced or groundwater) can significantly reduce anchor capacity in some cohesive soils (softer clays) with rotary drilling. Grout is generally placed by tremie or low-pressure methods; high-pressure post-grouting (150 psi or higher) fractures and expands the previously placed grout to compress the soil and form an enlarged bulb, increasing capacity, and is done through a separate ported grout tube. Because capacity varies widely, proof or performance tests are needed to confirm it; the FHWA/RD-82/047 report 'Tiebacks' provides capacity-estimating information. Bond capacity is the anchor's resistance to pull-out developed along the bonded length by the grout-soil interaction. The determination of the bonded length Lb and capacity is solely the Contractor's responsibility, verified by testing. The Engineer's review must include a check of the unbonded length: the minimum distance between the front of the bonded zone and the active failure surface behind the wall must not be less than H/5, in no case less than 5 feet, and the unbonded length must not be less than 15 feet (Figure 11-3). The ultimate anchor capacity is Pult = pi*d*Lb*Sb, where d is the drilled-hole diameter, Lb the bonded length, Lu the unbonded length, Sb the bond strength (lb/ft^2), and the assumed failure plane makes angle Psi = 45 - phi/2 with the vertical for the Rankine active condition. Bond strength depends on (1) location/effective overburden pressure above the anchor, (2) drilling method and hole configuration, (3) soil strength/type/relative density, (4) grouting method and pressure, and (5) tendon type/size/shape. Because bond strength is affected by the Contractor's means and methods, the assumed bond strength must be included in the submittal (preferably in a geotechnical report); Geotechnical Services (DES) are available for consultation.
key_points: Ultimate anchor capacity Pult = pi*d*Lb*Sb (d = hole diameter, Lb = bonded length, Sb = bond strength)
Bond (pull-out) capacity develops along the bonded length (grout-soil interaction)
Unbonded length check: front of bonded zone >= H/5 (and >= 5 ft) beyond the active surface; Lu >= 15 ft
Rankine active failure plane at Psi = 45 - phi/2 from vertical
Bond strength depends on overburden, drilling/hole shape, soil, grouting method/pressure, tendon
Post-grouting (>= 150 psi) forms an enlarged bulb and increases capacity
Under-reamed (belled) holes require cohesive soil; verify capacity by proof/performance testing

equations.description: Ultimate ground-anchor capacity Pult = pi*d*Lb*Sb (hole diameter d, bonded length Lb, bond strength Sb).
Front of bonded zone must be >= H/5 (and >= 5 ft) beyond the active failure surface; unbonded length Lu >= 15 ft.

sections.title: Forces on the Vertical Members
sections.summary: Inclined ground anchors impose a vertical force component that the vertical member must resist through skin friction on its embedded length and end bearing; failure to account for this downward load has caused excessive downward wall movement. Check the vertical capacity especially for (1) shoring in loose granular material or soft clays, (2) anchors steeper than the standard 15 degrees, and (3) multiple anchor rows; contact Caltrans Geotechnical Services for assistance.
sections.body: Ground anchors are generally inclined; therefore the vertical component of the ground anchor force must be resisted by the vertical member through skin friction on the embedded length of piling in contact with the soil and by end bearing. Problems with ground anchor walls have occurred because of excessive downward wall movement when this downward movement was not properly accounted for. The vertical capacity of the shoring system should be checked, particularly for (1) shoring embedded in loose granular material or soft clays, (2) ground anchors with angles steeper than the standard 15 degrees, and (3) when there are multiple rows of ground anchors. Contact Caltrans Geotechnical Services for assistance when checking the vertical capacity of the shoring elements.
key_points: Inclined anchors add a vertical (downward) force on the vertical member
Resisted by pile skin friction on the embedded length plus end bearing
Unaccounted downward load has caused excessive downward wall movement
Check vertical capacity for loose granular/soft clay, anchors steeper than 15 deg, and multiple anchor rows
sections.applicability: Checking the vertical (downdrag) capacity of anchored vertical members for inclined ground anchors

sections.title: Testing Temporary Ground Anchors (Proof and Performance Testing)
sections.summary: The Contractor verifies anchor capacity by testing after installation; testing matters most near existing structures or for long durations. Proof testing applies a sustained proof load (1.2-1.3 x design, or >= 1.3 high risk) and measures movement over a 10-60 min hold (by soil/risk; Table 11-1). Only the bonded length carries the proof load (unbonded length stays ungrouted). It is important to reach the proof load quickly; creep timing must begin when it is first reached. A 'lift-off test' is an alternative but cannot separate creep from wall movement; SC recommends a dial-indicator gauge. Performance testing (incremental load/unload) is not normally specified for temporary shoring.
sections.body: The Contractor is responsible for providing a reasonable test method for verifying anchor capacity after installation. Anchors are tested to verify they sustain the design load over time without excessive movement; testing is more important when supporting or adjacent to existing structures and for extended durations. The Contractor should consider the degree of risk in selecting the number of anchors tested, test duration, allowable movement, and allowable load loss; high-risk situations include where settlement or damage would affect adjacent facilities (Table 11-1 lists recommended minimum criteria). The shoring plans should include load testing criteria (minimally proof load values), frequency of testing, test load duration (to capture creep), allowable movement or load loss, anticipated service life, and remedial measures if test anchors fail. Pressure gauges/load cells should be recently calibrated (within one year), clean, and in good order. PROOF TESTING: applying a sustained proof load and measuring movement over a specified period is the typical method; it may begin after the grout reaches the desired strength. Table 11-1 gives recommended proof-test criteria: cohesionless soils normal risk 1.2-1.3 of design load, 10-min hold, 10% of anchors per soil type; cohesionless high risk >= 1.3 design load, 10 min, 20-100%; cohesive normal risk 1.2-1.3 design load, 30 min, 10%; cohesive high risk >= 1.3 design load, 60 min, 30-100%; adverse conditions (groundwater or soft clays) 60 min for 10% and 10 min for the remaining 90%. The unbonded length Lu is left ungrouted before and during testing so that only the bonded length Lb carries the proof load (grout in the unbonded zone lies within the failure wedge and would not contribute resistance, and could bear against the wall facing producing erroneous results); forensic work shows small-diameter anchors (<= 6 in) develop most capacity in the bonded length. An alignment load of 5-10% of the proof load secures the jack, then the load is increased to the proof load and the hold period begins; movement is measured with a dial indicator gauge on a tripod independent of the anchor and shoring (Figure 11-4), and continuous jacking maintains the proof load. The proof load must be reached quickly; if it takes too long or is held too long before measuring creep, the creep rate is not representative - the creep clock must start when the proof load is first reached. As an alternative, a 'lift-off test' compares the force at seating to the force at lift-off over a specified period; lost force converts to creep movement, but it cannot differentiate anchor creep from wall movement into the soil, so SC recommends a dial-indicator gauge instead. A ground anchor that does not satisfy the testing criteria may still have some value; the Contractor will need to revise the shoring plan (extra capacity of adjacent anchors, or an additional anchor). PERFORMANCE TESTING is more extensive (incremental loading/unloading with movement measurement) to establish movement behavior; it is not normally specified for temporary shoring but can identify causes of anchor movement. EVALUATION OF CREEP MOVEMENT (11-3.05C): long-term creep can be estimated from the proof-test measurements, the creep being roughly a logarithmic function of time. General formula for long term creep: Delta_2-3 = C*[log10(T3/T2)] (Eq. 11-3-1), where C = Delta_1-2/[log10(T2/T1)] (Eq. 11-3-2), a constant (typically in inches) from the movement between T1 (first measurement in the load hold, usually within 1 minute after the proof load is applied) and T2 (last measurement in the load hold); T3 is the time the shoring will be in use. If a lift-off test is used, Delta_1-2 = (P1 - P2)*Lu'/(AE) (Eq. 11-3-3) is substituted into Eq. 11-3-2, with P1 the force at seating, P2 the force at lift-off, Lu' = Lu + Delta_L (Delta_L = 3 to 5 ft of anchor length for the jack and wedges), A and E the area and modulus of the strand or bar. The formula is only an estimate of potential anchor creep, should be used with periodic monitoring of wall movement, and does not accurately predict anchor creep for soft cohesive soils.
key_points: Contractor verifies anchor capacity by proof testing (or performance testing) after installation
Proof load = 1.2-1.3 x design load (>= 1.3 for high risk); hold 10-60 min by soil type/risk (Table 11-1)
Only the bonded length Lb carries the proof load; the unbonded length stays ungrouted during testing
Reach the proof load quickly; start the creep clock when the proof load is first reached
Measure movement with a dial-indicator gauge independent of the anchor/shoring (Figure 11-4)
Lift-off test alternative cannot separate creep from wall movement; SC recommends the dial gauge
Performance testing (incremental load/unload) is not normally specified for temporary shoring
Long-term creep (11-3.05C): Delta_2-3 = C log10(T3/T2) (Eq. 11-3-1), C = Delta_1-2/log10(T2/T1) (Eq. 11-3-2); lift-off: Delta_1-2 = (P1 - P2)Lu'/(AE) (Eq. 11-3-3)

sections.title: Wall Movement and Settlement
sections.summary: As a rule of thumb, settlement of the soil behind a ground-anchor wall (with anchors locked off at a high percentage of design force) can be approximated as equal to the movement at the top of the wall from anchor creep plus pile deflection (see Section 7-3, System Deflection). Significant deflection/creep is unacceptable near existing structures where settlement is detrimental; where no permanent structures or sensitive features are affected, reasonable lateral movement and settlement may be tolerated.
sections.body: As a rule of thumb, the settlement of the soil behind a ground anchor wall, where the ground anchors are locked off at a high percentage of the design force, can be approximated as equal to the movement at the top of the wall caused by anchor creep and deflection of the piling (reference Section 7-3, System Deflection, of Chapter 7). If a shoring system is in close proximity to an existing structure where settlement might be detrimental, significant deflection and creep of the shoring system would not be acceptable. If a shoring system will not affect permanent structures, or supports something like a haul road, reasonable lateral movement and settlement may be tolerated.
key_points: Behind-wall settlement ~ top-of-wall movement (anchor creep + pile deflection) when locked off at high design force
Reference Section 7-3, System Deflection (Chapter 7)
Near sensitive existing structures, significant deflection/creep is unacceptable
Where no permanent structures are affected, reasonable movement/settlement may be tolerated
sections.applicability: Estimating soil settlement behind an anchored wall from wall movement and creep

sections.title: Lock-off Force
sections.summary: The lock-off force is the percentage of the required design force at which the anchor wedges/nut are seated after seating losses; 0.8*T_design is typically recommended (higher/lower values may be used for specific needs). For strand systems, a shim plate equal to the elastic elongation produced by (proof load - lock-off load) is inserted under the anchor head (corrected for wedge seating), Eq. 11-3-4 prints tshim = (Pproof - Plockoff)Lu'/(AE) - Delta_L. Seating loss is 0-1/16 in for threaded bars and 3/8-5/8 in for strands (often reduced by mechanically seating wedges).
sections.body: The lock-off force is the percentage of the required design force that the anchor wedges or anchor nut are seated at after seating losses. A value of 0.8*T_DESIGN is typically recommended as the lock-off force, but lower or higher values may be used to achieve specific design needs. One method for obtaining the proper lock-off force for strand systems is to insert a shim plate under the anchor head equal to the elastic elongation of the tendon produced by a force equal to the proof load minus the lock-off load, with a correction for wedge seating often subtracted from the shim thickness. The shim thickness may be found from Equation 11-3-4, printed as tshim = (Pproof - Plockoff)*Lu'/(A*E) - Delta_L, where tshim is the shim thickness, Pproof the proof load (kips), Plockoff the lock-off load (kips), A the tendon steel area (in^2), E the modulus of elasticity of the anchor (psi), Lu' the unbonded length of the anchor (ft), and Delta_L = 3 to 5 ft of anchor length necessary for the jack and anchor wedges. Note: Eq. 11-3-4 is stored as printed; it subtracts Delta_L, a length of 3 to 5 ft, from the shim thickness, whereas Section 11-3.05C (p. 11-16) and Example 11-1B (p. 11-20) use Delta_L in Lu' = Lu + Delta_L; the text before the equation says a correction for wedge seating is often subtracted from the shim thickness. Seating loss for threaded-bar systems is much less than for strands and can vary between 0 and 1/16 in; for strand systems it can vary between 3/8 and 5/8 in. The seating loss should be determined by the designer and verified during installation; mechanically seating the wedges minimizes seating loss. After seating the wedges at the proof load, the tendon is loaded, the shim removed, and the anchor head assembly seated against the bearing plate.
key_points: Lock-off force = fraction of design force at which the anchor is seated after seating loss; typically 0.8*T_design
Strand lock-off via a shim plate = elastic elongation from (Pproof - Plockoff); Eq. 11-3-4 prints tshim = (Pproof - Plockoff)Lu'/(AE) - Delta_L
Eq. 11-3-4 as printed subtracts Delta_L (3 to 5 ft for the jack and wedges); 11-3.05C defines Lu' = Lu + Delta_L
Seating loss: 0-1/16 in (threaded bars), 3/8-5/8 in (strands; less if wedges are mechanically seated)

equations.description: Shim plate thickness for strand lock-off, as printed: tshim = (Pproof - Plockoff)*Lu'/(A*E) - Delta_L (Pproof, Plockoff in kips; A in in^2; E in psi; Lu' unbonded length in ft; Delta_L = 3 to 5 ft for the jack and wedges). Section 11-3.05C uses Delta_L in Lu' = Lu + Delta_L instead.

sections.title: Corrosion Protection
sections.summary: The Contractor's submittal must address tendon corrosion after stressing. Very short-term installations on non-corrosive sites may not need protection. For longer-term installations, grouting the bonded and unbonded length is generally adequate on non-corrosive sites, with encapsulation/coating of un-grouted portions (anchor head, bearing plate, wedges, exposed strand). Long-term or corrosive-site installations may need elaborate schemes (grease as an inhibitor; pre-greased, pre-grouted plastic-sheathed tendons for permanent installations, Figure 11-5).
sections.body: The Contractor's submittal must address potential corrosion of the tendon after it has been stressed. For very short-term installations in non-corrosive sites, corrosion protection may not be necessary; the exposed steel may not be affected by a small amount of corrosion during its life. For longer-term installations, grouting of the bonded and unbonded length is generally adequate to minimize corrosion in most non-corrosive sites; encapsulating or coating any un-grouted portions (anchor head, bearing plate, wedges, strand, etc.) may be necessary. For long-term installations or installations in corrosive sites, more elaborate corrosion protection schemes may be necessary (grease is often used as a corrosion inhibitor). Figure 11-5 depicts tendons encapsulated in pre-greased and pre-grouted plastic sheaths generally used for permanent installations.
key_points: Submittal must address tendon corrosion after stressing
Very short-term, non-corrosive sites: protection may be unnecessary
Longer-term, non-corrosive: grout the bonded/unbonded length; encapsulate/coat un-grouted parts
Long-term or corrosive sites: elaborate schemes (grease inhibitor; pre-greased/pre-grouted sheathed tendons)

sections.title: General Steps for Checking Ground Anchor Shoring Submittal
sections.summary: A 12-step review checklist for an anchored-shoring submittal: review completeness; determine Ka and Kp (K0 if the wall cannot move sufficiently); develop pressure diagrams; determine forces; find the moment at the top of the pile above the highest anchor; solve for embedment depth D and anchor force TH (confirm D resists vertical loads); check the pile section; check anchor capacity; check miscellaneous details; check the anchor test procedure; review the corrosion proposal; and consider wall-deflection/settlement effects on surface features behind the wall.
sections.body: General steps for checking a ground anchor shoring submittal: (1) Review submittal for completeness. (2) Determine Ka and Kp; in the rare cases where the shoring is not allowed to move sufficiently, determine K0 in lieu of Ka. (3) Develop pressure diagrams. (4) Determine forces. (5) Determine the moments at the top of the pile above the highest ground anchor. (6) Solve for depth (D), for both lateral and ground anchor force (TH); confirm D is sufficient to resist the vertical loads. (7) Check pile section. (8) Check anchor capacity. (9) Check miscellaneous details. (10) Check adequacy of ground anchor test procedure. (11) Review corrosion proposal. (12) General: consider effects of wall deflection and subsequent soil settlement on any surface feature behind the shoring wall.
key_points: 12-step submittal-review checklist for anchored shoring
Determine Ka and Kp (K0 if the wall cannot move sufficiently)
Solve for embedment depth D and horizontal anchor force TH; confirm D resists vertical loads
Check the pile section, anchor capacity, details, test procedure, and corrosion proposal
Consider wall deflection/settlement effects on surface features behind the wall

sections.title: Estimating Long Term Creep
sections.summary: Section 11-3.10 states 'Determine the long-term effects of creep' and gives two examples applying the creep formulas of Section 11-3.05C (Eqs. 11-3-1 to 11-3-3). Example 11-1A (measurement and time): C = 0.1 inch/log10(10/1) = 0.1 inch (Eq. 11-3-6), Delta_2-3 = 0.1 log10(525,600/10) = 0.47 inches over 1 year (Eq. 11-3-7). Example '10-1B' as printed (lift-off load): Delta_1-2 = (83,000 - 67,900)(20)(12)/((0.647)(28x10^6)) ~ 0.2 inch, C ~ 0.063 inch, Delta_2-3 = 0.16 inch from 1 day to 365 days (Eqs. 11-3-8 to 11-3-11).
sections.body: Section 11-3.10 prints 'Determine the long-term effects of creep.' followed by two worked examples; the formulas they use are printed in Section 11-3.05C (pp. 11-15, 11-16): Delta_2-3 = C*[log10(T3/T2)] (Eq. 11-3-1), C = Delta_1-2/[log10(T2/T1)] (Eq. 11-3-2), and for a lift-off test Delta_1-2 = (P1 - P2)*Lu'/(AE) (Eq. 11-3-3), Lu' = Lu + Delta_L. These estimate potential anchor creep only, should be used with periodic monitoring of wall movement, and do not accurately predict creep for soft cohesive soils (11-3.05C). Example 11-1A, Measurement and Time Method (11-3.10A): the plans require the proof load to be applied in 2 minutes or less and held ten minutes, the test beginning on reaching the proof load; movements at 1, 4, 6, 8 and 10 minutes; proof load 133 percent of the design load; maximum permissible movement between 1 and 10 minutes 0.1 inch; all anchors tested; in place 1 year. T3 = (1Y)(365 D/Y)(24 H/D)(60 M/H) = 525,600 minutes (Eq. 11-3-5); C = 0.1 inch/[log10(10/1)] = 0.1 inch (Eq. 11-3-6); Delta_2-3 = (0.1) log10(525,600/10) = 0.47 inches (Eq. 11-3-7). The proof load and test duration exceed the Table 11-1 values; if the shoring were close to an existing structure that could not tolerate 1/2 inch of wall deflection, the design may not be acceptable, while where it will not affect permanent structures the movement may be acceptable. Example '10-1B' as printed, Lift-Off Load Method (11-3.10B; the heading prints 10-1B, not 11-1B): lift-off test 24 hours after the wedges are seated; force at seating 83,000 lb, lift-off force no less than 67,900 lb; Lu' = Lu + Delta_L ~ 20 ft (15 ft unbonded + 5 ft in the jack); A = 0.647 in^2; E = 28x10^6 psi; T1 = 1 minute. Delta_1-2 = (P1 - P2)Lu'/(AE) (Eq. 11-3-8) ~ (83,000 - 67,900)(20)(12)/((0.647)(28x10^6)) ~ 0.2 inch (Eq. 11-3-9); C ~ 0.2/[log10((24)(60)/1)] = 0.063 inch (Eq. 11-3-10); with T2 = 1 day and T3 = 365 days, Delta_2-3 ~ (0.063 inch) log10(365 days/1 day) (Eq. 11-3-11) = 0.16 inch.
key_points: 11-3.10 gives two examples of the creep formulas printed in 11-3.05C (Eqs. 11-3-1 to 11-3-3)
Lift-off: Delta_1-2 = (P1 - P2)Lu'/(AE) (Eq. 11-3-3), Lu' = Lu + Delta_L
Estimate only; does not accurately predict creep in soft cohesive soils; use with periodic wall-movement monitoring
Example 11-1A: 0.47 inch over 1 year (Eq. 11-3-7); Example '10-1B' (as printed, lift-off): 0.16 inch from 1 to 365 days

equations.description: General formula for long term creep, Delta_2-3 = C[log10(T3/T2)], with C = Delta_1-2/[log10(T2/T1)] (Eq. 11-3-2); printed in Section 11-3.05C, p. 11-16.
Lift-off test approximation substituted into Eq. 11-3-2: Delta_1-2 = (P1 - P2)Lu'/(AE), P1 force at seating, P2 force at lift-off, Lu' = Lu + Delta_L; printed in Section 11-3.05C, p. 11-16.

sections.title: Construction (Inspection Considerations)
sections.summary: Shoring integrity depends on design adequacy, material quality, and workmanship; frequent, thorough inspection by qualified personnel is required at all stages. A 23-item checklist of common construction/inspection considerations covers permits, plan familiarity, soil/groundwater monitoring, distress indicators, member sizes/spacing and sequence, ground-anchor installation, cable thimbles/clamps, surcharge monitoring, weather, vibrations, utility notification (USA 811) within 5x the excavation depth, benchmarks for ground-movement monitoring, egress within 25 ft, hazardous-atmosphere protection, and competent-person daily inspections.
sections.body: The integrity of a shoring system depends on the adequacy of the design, the quality of materials, and the quality of workmanship; frequent, thorough inspection by qualified personnel is required during all stages of construction. Common considerations (23-item list) include: confirm a current Cal/OSHA excavation permit (annual permits Jan 1-Dec 31, or project-specific); become familiar with the authorized plans, location, assumptions, soils data, groundwater, surcharge loads, sequence, utilities, and the Contractor's competent person; know the minimum safety requirements; assess excavated soil against the Log of Test Borings; monitor groundwater; watch for distress (tension cracks, subsidence); inspect sloped (unshored) cuts especially after rain; verify shored member size/spacing and follow the plan sequence; check full bearing at jacks/struts; review materials for quality and grade; use manufactured products per manufacturer recommendations; install ground anchors per the authorized plan; use thimbles and proper cable clamps (no sharp corners); monitor surcharge loads; account for weather effects on clays; maintain good workmanship; add monitoring for dynamic loads (vibratory compaction, pile driving, blasting); notify utility owners (Underground Service Alert / 811) when facilities are within 5x the excavation depth; use benchmarks to monitor horizontal/vertical ground movement; provide egress (ladders/ramps/stairs) in excavations 4 ft or deeper within 25 ft of lateral travel; protect against hazardous atmospheres (air monitoring, confined-space rules); protect employees from accumulating water, falling debris, and unstable structures; the Contractor's competent person performs daily and post-storm inspections with authority to remove endangered workers; and provide barrier protection and backfill temporary shafts/pits. Contractor-proposed alternative systems (wire-mesh MSE, 'burrito' retention, proprietary systems) are reviewed against the manufacturer's published design criteria.
key_points: Shoring integrity = design adequacy + material quality + workmanship; inspect at all stages
Verify a current Cal/OSHA excavation permit and follow the plan's sequence of operations
Monitor groundwater, surcharge loads, distress (tension cracks/subsidence), and dynamic loads
Notify Underground Service Alert (811) for utilities within 5x the excavation depth
Provide egress in excavations >= 4 ft (within 25 ft of lateral travel) and hazardous-atmosphere protection
Competent person performs daily and post-storm inspections with authority to remove workers
sections.applicability: Inspecting and monitoring shoring systems during construction

sections.title: Encroachment Permit Projects
sections.summary: An encroachment permit (issued by the District Permit Engineer) is required for work by others within or adjacent to State highway right-of-way. If excavation/shoring is involved, shoring plans must accompany the application and be authorized before the permit issues; complex systems may be routed to Structure Maintenance, Bridge Design, or Structure Construction. A California-registered civil engineer must prepare plans that deviate from Title 8 safety orders. The minimum shoring-plan content (permit number, contractor/owner, location, purpose, soil profile, surcharge loadings, the shoring plan, manufactured data, construction permit, and the competent person) is enumerated.
sections.body: An encroachment permit is required for projects performed by others within State highway right-of-way or adjacent to State highways (including cooperative agreements such as Capital Improvement Projects); the Contractor, builder, or owner must apply to the District Permit Engineer. If the scope requires excavation and shoring, plans must accompany the application and be reviewed/authorized by the District Permit Engineer before a permit is issued. The plan may be routed to Structure Maintenance, Bridge Design, or Structure Construction for review, and must conform to Chapter 2 (Cal/OSHA Overview) and the permit application. Acceptance is based on what is required for a State project, with consideration of the Contractor's background, the work, and the degree of risk; geotechnical engineering is not an exact science. The minimum shoring-plan content includes: Encroachment Permit No.; Contractor (name, address, phone); Owner (and contract number); Owner Encroachment Permit No.; Location; Purpose; Soil Profile (basis of identification); Surcharge Loadings (all adjacent loads with dimensions; the minimum surcharge applies where not exceeded); the Excavation/Trenching & Shoring Plan (a letter for simple work, a full description for complex systems - and per the California Labor Code, plans deviating from Title 8 safety orders must be prepared and signed by a California-registered civil engineer); Manufactured Data; Construction Permit (Cal/OSHA); and Inspection (the designated competent person). The Engineer reviews the plan per applicable specifications and the Construction Safety Orders, considering deviations with adequate supporting data. The District Encroachment Permit Engineer is responsible for fieldwork inspection; complex work may require Structure Construction assistance acting as a representative of the District Permit Engineer, who can withdraw the permit to stop work.
key_points: Encroachment permit (District Permit Engineer) required for work in/adjacent to State highway right-of-way
Shoring plans must accompany the application and be authorized before the permit issues
Plans deviating from Title 8 safety orders must be prepared/signed by a California-registered civil engineer
Minimum plan content includes soil profile, surcharge loadings, the shoring plan, manufactured data, permits, and the competent person
Review per specifications and the Construction Safety Orders; SC may assist the District Permit Engineer
sections.applicability: Reviewing shoring plans submitted under an encroachment permit

sections.title: Summary
sections.summary: Closing summary: the Department has legal obligations for trenching/shoring (Chapters 1 and 2); soil mechanics is not a precise science, so be aware of assumptions; simplified analysis procedures suffice for much of the work; construction quality is as important as design; and railroad work needs additional controls. Key procedural points: a California-registered engineer must review Contractor temporary-structure plans; the Contractor must hold a posted Cal/OSHA permit; trenches <= 20 ft following Cal/OSHA standard details need no independent analysis, but deeper trenches or deviations from the standard details require professional-engineer plans and an independent analysis.
sections.body: The Department has an obligation with respect to trenching and shoring work; be informed of legal responsibilities (Chapter 1, Legal Requirements, and Chapter 2, Cal/OSHA Overview). Soil mechanics (geotechnical engineering) is not a precise science; be aware of the effects assumptions can make. Simplified engineering analysis procedures can be used for much of the trenching and shoring work encountered. The actual construction work is of equal importance to the design; the Contractor and Engineer must be alert to changing conditions and take appropriate action - good engineering judgment is essential. Railroad work requires additional controls and specific administrative procedures. Summary of requirements: (1) State Statute Sec. 137.6 requires a California-registered engineer to review the Contractor's plans for temporary structures (including shoring plans) on State highway work; (2) the Engineer confirms a proper Cal/OSHA excavation/trenching permit is obtained and posted before work starts; (3) trenches <= 20 ft deep that conform to Cal/OSHA Construction Safety Order standard details need not be prepared by a professional engineer and need no independent analysis (the Engineer confirms conformance); (4) trenches over 20 ft, or where the standard details do not apply, must have plans prepared by a professional engineer; (5) plans deviating from the Cal/OSHA CSO must be prepared by a California-registered professional engineer and the reviewer performs an independent analysis; (6) designs by specialty firms may appear less conservative and may need to be reviewed in the manner designed (obtain SC Falsework Engineer assistance); (7) railroad-authorization work is handled through the SC Falsework Engineer as liaison; (8) revisions should be done by the plan originator.
key_points: The Department has legal obligations for trenching/shoring (Chapters 1 and 2)
Geotechnical engineering is not a precise science; be aware of assumptions
Construction quality is as important as design; railroad work needs additional controls
A California-registered engineer reviews Contractor temporary-structure (shoring) plans; Cal/OSHA permit must be posted
Trenches <= 20 ft per Cal/OSHA standard details need no independent analysis; deeper trenches or deviations require PE plans and independent analysis
sections.applicability: Summarizing Caltrans trenching/shoring review requirements and procedures
